record.name: Wuliangshan Gushu Shou
record.origin: Wuliang Mountain, Jingdong County, Pu'er City, Yunnan, China

paragraphs.text: This cake comes from [Wuliang Mountain](wuliang-mountain:where), a long range in west-central Yunnan rather than a single peak. It runs south from Nanjian in Dali, past Jingdong, Zhenyuan and Jinggu, and fades out toward Xishuangbanna. The leaf is from Jingdong County, one of the two counties most often named for the range's [old tea trees](wuliang-mountain:trees), which grow wild in the forest and as older plantings in village gardens.

It was made into [ripe pu'er](shou:definition) and pressed in 2019. The leaf was wetted and heaped in a [fermenting pile](shou:wet-piling), covered to hold in the heat its own microbes make, and turned about once a week to let air in. The pile exists to give in weeks what raw pu'er reaches only after years of waiting, so a ripe cake is ready soon after it is made.
At seven years the cake has entered the [settling years](shou:age-settling) of the style, the stretch between about five and ten years when what the pile left behind has usually aired away.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, sweet cup with earthy or woody notes. A young ripe tea can carry a faint smell of the pile, which fades with airing or in the first steeps.
